title: Hook
text: Imagine pushing a giant concrete wall all day long. You sweat, you pant, your muscles ache. You feel exhausted. But a physicist walks by and says: 'You haven't done any work at all!' How is that possible?

title: Socratic Thinking
text: Why do you think the physicist says no work was done, even though you used so much effort? What is missing from the scientific definition of work?

content.title: Pushing a Wall vs. Pushing a Cart
content.description: Notice that the wall doesn't move, but the cart does.

title: Reveal
text: In physics, Work is only done when a force is applied to an object, and the object moves in the direction of the force. The formula is Work (W) = Force (F) × Displacement (s). If there is no displacement (like pushing the wall), the work done is exactly zero!

content.question: If you push a heavy box with a force of 100 N and it doesn't move, how much work have you done?

title: Reflection
text: Think about it: can you explain to your friend why carrying a heavy bag and standing still for an hour involves no 'work' in a scientific sense, even though it makes you tired?

title: Connection
text: Work is intimately connected to Energy. When you do work on an object, you transfer energy to it. In future sections, we'll see how this energy can be Kinetic (energy of motion) or Potential (stored energy).

content.title: Mastery Challenge
content.description: Calculate the work done when a force of 50 N moves a chair by 2 meters across the room. (Hint: W = F x s). Try calculating it before moving to the next section!

content.text: Always remember that displacement must be in the direction of the force. If you carry a bag and walk forward, the force you apply to hold the bag is upwards, but movement is forwards. So, the work done against gravity is zero!

content.mistake: Confusing mental or physical tiredness with scientific work.
content.correction: Scientific work requires both an applied force and a displacement in the direction of that force.
